title: Black Holes That Predate the Big Bang
hook: If our universe expanded out of an earlier contracting one rather than from nothing, black holes could have survived the handover — cosmic fossils that might also be the dark matter.
key_points: In a 'bounce' cosmology, the Big Bang is not the beginning but the turnaround of a previous contracting phase.
A new model argues black holes formed before that turnaround could survive the bounce intact.
Such relics would be older than the Big Bang itself, in the sense of predating the start of our expansion.
They offer two payoffs at once: a candidate for dark matter, and an explanation for surprisingly massive objects seen very early in cosmic history.
This is a model, not an observation — the test would be whether the predicted mass distribution of relics matches what surveys find.
content_html: The Big Bang is usually told as the beginning of everything. Bounce cosmologies tell it differently: the universe was contracting, reached a minimum size, and rebounded — so what we call the Big Bang is a turnaround in a longer story. That reframing raises an obvious question. If anything existed before the bounce, could it get through?
extra_html: A new model, reported via ScienceDaily, argues that black holes could. Formed during the contracting phase, they would survive the transition and still be roaming the universe today as cosmic fossils — objects older than the Big Bang in the sense of predating our expansion. The appeal is that one population would settle two separate puzzles. As dark, massive, and effectively invisible objects, the relics are a dark matter candidate; and because they would already be in place when our expansion began, they could explain why surprisingly massive objects show up so early in cosmic history, a tension that telescopes such as Webb have sharpened. The caution is the usual one for pre-Big-Bang scenarios: this is a theoretical construction rather than a detection, and it earns its keep only if the predicted population — how many relics, at what masses — matches what surveys and gravitational-wave detectors actually see.

related.title: The Big Bang
related.hook: About 13.8 billion years ago the universe began hot and dense and has been expanding ever since — but it wasn't an explosion into empty space. Space itself stretched.

related.title: Could This Odd LIGO Signal Be the Missing Dark Matter?
related.hook: An unusual gravitational-wave signal has revived a long-shot idea: that primordial black holes born moments after the Big Bang could be the universe's missing dark matter.

related.title: Did Clusters of Primordial Black Holes Seed JWST's Puzzling 'Little Red Dots'?
related.hook: JWST found overweight black holes far too early in the universe for standard theories to explain. One proposal: they were seeded by swarms of black holes born moments after the Big Bang.

flashcards.prompt: What does a 'bounce' cosmology replace the Big Bang singularity with?
flashcards.back_html: A turnaround: the universe was contracting, reached a minimum, and rebounded into the expansion we observe — so the Big Bang is a transition, not a beginning.

flashcards.prompt: Why would black holes surviving a cosmic bounce be scientifically attractive?

choices.text: They could account for dark matter and for very massive objects appearing surprisingly early
They would prove the universe is younger than currently believed
They would remove the need for gravity to be quantum

flashcards.explanation_html: The relics do double duty in the model: an unseen mass component behaving like dark matter, plus a head start that explains early massive objects.

flashcards.prompt: In what sense can a black hole be 'older than the Big Bang'?
flashcards.back_html: It formed during the earlier contracting phase and persisted through the bounce, so it predates the start of our universe's expansion.
